deep.reconstruction:
This page is a 5-place table of Gaussian (addition) logarithms. In Gauss's own published layout, the argument is A = log10 x. The 'value' column is B(A) = log10(1 + 1/x) = log10(1 + 10^(-A)). The 'sum' column is C = A + B = log10(1 + x) = log10(1 + 10^A). The two smaller columns are first differences between successive tabulated B and C values, written between the lines, in units of 1e-5. The page covers A = 0.720 to 0.800 in steps of 0.001, in two blocks (0.720–0.760 and 0.760–0.800), grouped in fives.

The page continues fol. 17 (A = 0.640–0.720) and leads into fol. 19 (A = 0.800–0.880).

The purpose is to find log(a+b) from log a and log b without leaving logarithms. Set A = log a − log b. Then log(a+b) = log b + C(A) = log a + B(A). Equivalently, for differences, one can enter the table with C and read A or B.

Worked checks (mine):
- A = 0.720: x = 10^0.72 = 5.24807; log10(1 + 0.190546) = 0.075749, so B = 0.07575 and C = 0.79575.
- A = 0.760: x = 5.75440; B = log10(1.173780) = 0.069587, so 0.06959; C = 0.82959.
- A = 0.800: x = 6.30957; B = log10(1.158489) = 0.063893, so 0.06389; C = 0.86389.

The structure has internal consistency checks: C − A = B exactly in every row, and ΔB + ΔC = 0.001 (100 units), e.g. 16 + 84 and 15 + 85. Every row on the page satisfies these. As expected, the B-differences shrink from 16 to 14/13 because dB/dA = −1/(1 + x).
errors: No computational errors found. Spot checks against exact values agree to the last place, including the near-tie cases. At A = 0.759, exact B = 0.0697349, tabulated 0.06973. At A = 0.776, exact B = 0.0672548, tabulated 0.06725; this is a visibly corrected entry. At A = 0.740, exact B = 0.072606, tabulated 0.07261.
All B and C differences are consistent with the tabulated values, and C = A + B holds in every row.

results.what: Table of B(A) = log10(1 + 10^-A) and C(A) = A + B = log10(1 + 10^A) for A = 0.720..0.800, 5 decimals, with first differences
results.usually_credited_to: Z. Leonelli (idea, 1802/1803); C. F. Gauss, who published a 5-place table in Zach's Monatliche Correspondenz, 1812

deep.surprise_reason: This is a manuscript sheet of the Gaussian-logarithm table that Gauss published in 1812 and that bears his name. It is routine computational work, of interest only as a working draft showing his corrections and difference checks.
